title: Aristotle's Golden Mean
objective: After this level you can explain Aristotle's virtue ethics, where courage sits between cowardice and recklessness and virtue is built by practice.
summary: Aristotle placed each virtue at a mean between two vices, relative to the person, as courage lies between cowardice and rashness, and held that virtue is built by practice.

cards.headline: Is the bravest person the one who feels no fear?
cards.body: Aristotle said no. Feeling too little fear is a failure too, just a louder one.

cards.headline: Between two mistakes
cards.body: For Aristotle, each virtue is a mean between a vice of excess and a vice of deficiency. Courage is his example. The coward flees every danger, with too much fear. The rash person thinks every danger worth facing and feels little or no fear. The courageous person sits between them, facing the right dangers with the right amount of fear.

cards.headline: Six isn’t the answer
cards.body: The mean isn’t the arithmetic middle. If 10 pounds of food is too much and 2 too little, a trainer won’t just order 6. For Milo, the athlete, that would be too little; for a beginner, too much. The mean is relative to us: right for this person, here. And some acts, like theft and murder, have no mean at all. They’re always wrong.

mascot.line: People mix these up: the mean isn’t the average. It’s the right amount for you, in your situation.

cards.headline: Brave by doing brave things
cards.body: How do you get there? Practice. People become builders by building and harp-players by playing the harp. In the same way, Aristotle argued, we become just by doing just acts and brave by doing brave ones. That’s why lawmakers try to make citizens good by training their habits. Virtue is less a gift than a skill.

cards.headline: But what should I do?
cards.body: A common criticism: virtue ethics answers “What sort of person should I be?” but not “What should I do?” The philosopher Rosalind Hursthouse replied that virtue words already guide action: do what is honest or charitable; don’t do what is dishonest. And our list of vice words, from lazy to inconsiderate, is remarkably long.

cards.headline: Aristotle’s Golden Mean: the big picture
learned: Each virtue is a mean between two vices
The mean is relative to the person
Virtue grows by practice, like building

questions.prompt: Where does Aristotle place the virtue of courage?

options.label: Between rashness and recklessness
options.rationale: Those are both excesses of daring.

options.label: Anywhere a person feels no fear

questions.explanation: Courage is the mean between cowardice, too much fear, and rashness, too little.

questions.prompt: Why wouldn’t Aristotle’s trainer order the same 6 pounds of food for every athlete?

options.label: Food was too scarce in ancient Greece
Six is too close to ten
options.rationale: The problem isn’t the number itself.

options.label: The right amount is relative to each person
Athletes should always eat the most they can
options.rationale: That’s the excess, not the mean.

questions.explanation: The mean is relative to us: 6 pounds would be too little for Milo and too much for a beginner.

questions.prompt: Xunzi compared becoming good to a potter shaping clay. What does Aristotle’s point about builders share with it?

options.label: Goodness is inborn and needs no effort
options.rationale: Both deny that goodness comes without effort.

options.label: Only craftsmen can be good
options.rationale: The craft is a comparison, not a job requirement.

options.label: Goodness is acquired by practice, like a craft

questions.explanation: Both compare goodness to a craft: Xunzi’s pot needs a potter, and Aristotle’s builders learn by building, as we become just by doing just acts.
